---
title: "Grouped ecological response curves"
---

```{r}
#| include: false
# Load ggplot2 for the consistently formatted rendered figures in this chapter.
library(ggplot2)
```

# Introduction

In this chapter, we learn how to fit response curves to observations that come in groups.
Repeated measurements on the same plants, animals, nests or sites share the conditions of
their group, so they are not independent of each other. A grouped model describes three
things together: a curve that is common to all the groups, how that curve varies among
groups, and how the observations vary around the curve of their own group. The variation
among groups is described by a probability distribution, and the model is fitted by
maximum likelihood once the deviations of the groups have been integrated out of the
likelihood.

What is new in this chapter is the conditional distribution, which describes the two levels
of such a model, and the marginal distribution that follows from it; random effects and
partial pooling, with which a grouped model shares information among groups; maximum
marginal likelihood and the Laplace approximation, with which the model is fitted; variance
components and shrinkage; restricted maximum likelihood (REML), which reduces the bias of
the estimated variances; the curves of observed and of new groups; and how grouped models
are checked and compared. One example runs through the chapter, the uptake of carbon
dioxide (CO₂) by 12 plants of a grass, each measured at seven concentrations of CO₂
(Potvin et al. 1990).^[Potvin, C., Lechowicz, M. J. and Tardif, S. (1990), "The
statistical analysis of ecophysiological response curves obtained from experiments
involving repeated measures", *Ecology* 71: 1389–1400. The data are in R as `CO2`.] The
curve is the saturating exponential and the observations follow a Normal distribution. RTMB
integrates the deviations of the groups out of the likelihood when we give `MakeADFun()`
the argument `random`. [Chapter 6](../Chapter_6/Theory.qmd) treated every observation as
independent; [Chapter 8](../Chapter_8/Theory.qmd) deals with the difficulties of finding the
maximum of a likelihood.

# Learning goals

In this chapter, we will cover:

- observations in groups;
- conditional and marginal distributions;
- fixed and random effects;
- complete, no and partial pooling;
- the marginal likelihood and the Laplace approximation;
- random effects in RTMB;
- variance components and predicted group effects;
- group-level predictors and shrinkage;
- the uncertainty of variance components and REML;
- curves for observed and new groups;
- checking a grouped model;
- comparing grouped models with AIC and leave-one-group-out cross-validation.

We will use the [Normal](../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-normal) entry of the
distribution supplement and the
[saturating exponential](../Supplements/deterministic-functions.qmd#sec-fn-monomolecular)
entry of the function supplement.

The table below is a roadmap of the chapter. Each row is one step, with the question that
it answers and the R tools that we use for it.

| Step | Question it answers | In R |
|---|---|---|
| The groups | Which observations share the conditions of a group? | an integer index of the group of each observation |
| The model | How does the curve vary among groups, and how do the observations vary around it? | the deviations of the groups as a vector in the list of parameters |
| Pooling | Should the groups share one curve, have curves of their own, or something in between? | one NLL for each choice |
| The fit | Which parameter values make the observations most probable, once the deviations of the groups are integrated out? | `MakeADFun()` with `random`, `optim()`, `sdreport()` |
| Predictors | Do properties of the groups explain part of the variation among them? | fixed effects on the parameter that varies, `ADREPORT()` |
| Uncertainty and REML | How precisely are the variances estimated, and how biased are they? | `TMB::tmbprofile()`, `random` with the fixed effects |
| New groups | Which curves do we expect for groups that were not measured? | the distribution of the group deviations, `qnorm()` |
| Checking | Does the fitted model describe the observations and the groups? | `OBS()`, `obj$simulate()`, `DHARMa::recalculateResiduals()` |
| Comparison | Which of the candidate models do the data support? | AIC, `map` in `MakeADFun()`, a `for` loop that leaves out one group at a time |

: Roadmap of the chapter.

# Observations in groups {#sec-grouped-observations}

The **observational unit** is the entity on which one observation is made, such as a
quadrat, a visit to a nest or a measurement on a plant. In Chapters 4 and 6 the observations
were independent. Often, however, observations come in **groups** (also called grouping
units): several observations are made on the same individual, at the same site, in the same
nest or in the same tank. The observations of one group share conditions that other groups
do not share (the genotype and condition of an individual, the microhabitat of a site, the
parents of a brood, the observer of a survey), so they tend to resemble each other more than
observations of different groups do. The variation among groups is part of the process
variation of [Chapter 1](../Chapter_1/Theory.qmd): it would remain with perfect
measurements.

Treating grouped observations as independent overstates the information in the data.
Another observation of a group that we have already observed tells us less than an
observation of a new group, because part of what it shows is the condition of its group,
which we already know something about. A model that treats every observation as
independent therefore calculates standard errors that are too small and intervals that are
too narrow, and the evidence for an effect looks stronger than it is. The
[practical of Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Practicals/no_solution.qmd) met this problem with
tadpoles that share a tank, and
[Chapter 6](../Chapter_6/Theory.qmd#sec-response-comparison) used the number of tanks and
not the number of tadpoles as the number of observations in AICc and BIC for the same
reason. A grouped model describes the dependence explicitly: each group has a curve of its
own, and a distribution describes how the curves vary among groups.

The data of this chapter come from an experiment on the cold tolerance of the grass
*Echinochloa crus-galli*. Six plants came from Quebec and six from Mississippi, and three
plants of each origin were chilled overnight before the measurements. The CO₂ uptake of
every plant (µmol/m²/s) was measured at the same seven ambient concentrations of CO₂,
from 95 to 1000 µL/L,^[The help page of `CO2` gives the concentration in mL/L, but the
units stored with the data set (`attr(CO2, "units")`) are µL/L, which is the same as
parts per million (ppm). An ambient concentration of 1000 mL/L would be pure CO₂.] so the
design has 2 origins × 2 treatments × 3 plants × 7 concentrations, 84 measurements in
total. The observational unit is one measurement and the group is the plant.

The uptake rises with the concentration and levels off (@fig-co2_data). We describe it with
the [saturating exponential](../Supplements/deterministic-functions.qmd#sec-fn-monomolecular)
shifted along $x$ (see "Shifting and scaling" in
[Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-shifts)):

$$
\mu(x)=a\left(1-e^{-b(x-c)}\right),
$$

where $\mu(x)$ is the expected uptake (µmol/m²/s) at the concentration $x$ (µL/L), $a$ is
the asymptote (µmol/m²/s), $b$ is the rate at which the curve approaches it (L/µL), and $c$
is the concentration at which the expected uptake is zero (µL/L). The curve reaches 63% of
its asymptote at $x=c+1/b$ (see the supplement entry). The measurements start at 95 µL/L,
so we use the curve above $c$ only. The asymptote is the uptake of a plant at high
concentrations of CO₂, a measure of its capacity for photosynthesis, and it is the property
in which the plants of @fig-co2_data differ most visibly, so it is the parameter that we
will let vary among plants.

The data set `CO2` is stored as a special kind of data frame for grouped data, which we
turn into an ordinary data frame with `as.data.frame()`. Its column
`Plant` names the plant of each measurement: the first letter is the origin (Q or M), the
second the treatment (n for non-chilled, c for chilled), and the number distinguishes the
three plants of each combination. `Plant` is an ordered factor whose levels are not in the
order of the rows, so we build the integer index of the plants ourselves, with `match()`,
numbering the plants in the order in which they first appear. Plants 1 to 3 are then the
non-chilled plants from Quebec, 4 to 6 the chilled ones, 7 to 9 the non-chilled plants from
Mississippi and 10 to 12 the chilled ones. The list of data holds the concentration, the
uptake and the index of the plant of each measurement:

```{r}
#| message: false
# Load RTMB first and RTMBdist second.
library(RTMB)
library(RTMBdist)

# CO2 uptake of 12 plants at seven concentrations (see ?CO2), as an ordinary data frame.
co2 = as.data.frame(CO2)

# Names of the plants in the order of the rows, and the index (1 to 12) of the plant of
# each measurement.
plant_names = unique(as.character(co2$Plant))
plant = match(as.character(co2$Plant), plant_names)
plant_names

# List of data: the predictor, the response and the plant of each measurement.
co2_data = list(conc = co2$conc, uptake = co2$uptake, plant = plant)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-co2_data
#| fig-cap: "CO₂ uptake of 12 plants of *Echinochloa crus-galli* against the ambient concentration of CO₂, in four panels for the two origins and the two treatments. Lines join the measurements of the same plant; the line type and symbol distinguish the three plants of each panel."
# Measurements with the number of each plant within its origin and treatment.
co2_plot = co2
co2_plot$plant_number = substr(as.character(co2_plot$Plant), 3, 3)
co2_plot$Treatment = factor(co2_plot$Treatment, labels = c("Non-chilled", "Chilled"))

ggplot(co2_plot, aes(x = conc, y = uptake, group = Plant)) +
  geom_line(aes(linetype = plant_number), colour = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = plant_number), colour = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
  facet_grid(Treatment ~ Type) +
  labs(
    x = expression("Ambient CO"[2] * " concentration (µL/L)"),
    y = expression("CO"[2] * " uptake (µmol/m²/s)"),
    linetype = "Plant",
    shape = "Plant"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

# Conditional and marginal distributions {#sec-conditional}

[Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-joint-independence) introduced the joint
distribution of two random variables, the marginal distribution of each of them and
independence. The **conditional distribution** of $X_1$ for a given value $x_2$ of $X_2$
gives the probabilities of the values of $X_1$ among the outcomes in which $X_2=x_2$:

$$
P(X_1=x_1\mid X_2=x_2)=\frac{P(X_1=x_1,X_2=x_2)}{P(X_2=x_2)},
$$

where the numerator is the joint probability and the denominator the marginal probability
of the given value, which must be larger than zero. The bar reads "for a given value of",
as in the likelihood notation of [Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-likelihood); what
is given now is the value of another random variable. In the table of the two seeds of
Chapter 2, with $P(X_1=1)=0.6$ and $P(X_2=1)=0.3$, the probability that the first seed does
not germinate, for a given failure of the second, is

$$
P(X_1=0\mid X_2=0)=\frac{0.28}{0.70}=0.4,
$$

which equals the marginal probability $P(X_1=0)=0.4$. This is what independence means:
the conditional distribution of $X_1$ is the same for every value of $X_2$, and equal to
the marginal distribution, so knowing $X_2$ does not change the probabilities of $X_1$.
When the two variables are not independent, the conditional distribution changes with the
given value (@imp-seedlings-quadrat).

Multiplying both sides of the definition by $P(X_2=x_2)$ writes the joint distribution as
a conditional distribution times a marginal one,

$$
P(X_1=x_1,X_2=x_2)=P(X_1=x_1\mid X_2=x_2)\,P(X_2=x_2),
$$

and adding these joint probabilities over all the values of $X_2$ gives the marginal
distribution of $X_1$, as in the tables of Chapter 2. For continuous random variables the
same relations hold with densities in place of probabilities and an integral in place of
the sum
([Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-two_continuous_variables)):

$$
f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)},
\qquad
f_{X,Y}(x,y)=f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\,f_Y(y),
\qquad
f_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\,f_Y(y)\,dy,
$$

where $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)$ is the conditional density of $X$ for a given value $y$ of
$Y$. In plain English, the marginal density of $X$ is the average of its conditional
densities over all the values of $Y$, each weighted by the density of that value. This is
the form in which a grouped model is written: first the distribution of the value of a
group, then the distribution of the observations for a given value; the marginal
distribution of the observations follows by integration.

We have met a marginal distribution of this kind before. The Beta-Binomial distribution of
[Chapter 6](../Chapter_6/Theory.qmd#sec-beta-binomial-fit) is the marginal distribution of a
count that is Binomial for a given probability, when the probability varies among sampling
units according to a Beta distribution: each reed frog tank had its own probability that a
tadpole was killed, and the Beta-Binomial distribution describes the counts with those
probabilities integrated out. For this combination of distributions the integral has a
closed form, which is why we could write its probability mass directly. A **random effect**
is the same idea with a Normal distribution for the value of each group, usually on a
transformed scale (the logarithm of a positive parameter or the logit of a probability).
For most such models the integral has no closed form, and we need the approximation of
@sec-marginal-likelihood.

In general, let $Y_{ij}$ be the $i$-th observation of group $j$ and $u_j$ the deviation of
group $j$ from the common curve. For the CO₂ data the model is

$$
u_j\sim\operatorname{Normal}\left(0,\sigma^2_{\mathrm{plant}}\right),
\qquad
Y_{ij}\mid u_j\sim\operatorname{Normal}\left(\mu_j(x_{ij}),\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}\right),
\qquad
\mu_j(x)=a\,e^{u_j}\left(1-e^{-b(x-c)}\right),
$$

where $j=1,\ldots,12$ are the plants and $i=1,\ldots,7$ the measurements of a plant,
$x_{ij}$ is the concentration of measurement $i$ of plant $j$, $u_j$ is the deviation of
plant $j$ on the log scale of the asymptote, $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{plant}}$ is the variance of
these deviations among plants, $\mu_j(x)$ is the curve of plant $j$, and
$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}$ is the variance of the measurements around the curve of their
plant. The asymptote of plant $j$ is $a_j=a\,e^{u_j}$, that is,
$\log(a_j)=\log(a)+u_j$, so every asymptote is positive and the deviations act by
multiplication: a plant with $u_j=0.1$ has an asymptote about 10% above $a$ (because
$e^{0.1}\approx1.105$). The rate $b$ and the location $c$ are shared by all plants.

The model has two levels. For a given value of $u_j$, the seven measurements of plant $j$
are independent: each varies around the curve of its plant with variance
$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}$. Marginally, that is, without knowing $u_j$, they are not
independent, because they share $u_j$: a measurement above the common curve makes it more
probable that the plant has a high asymptote, and so that its other measurements are also
above the common curve. This is the dependence of grouped observations described in
@sec-grouped-observations, now written as a model. Measurements of different plants are
independent, because the deviations of different plants are independent.

The parameters that are shared by all the groups ($a$, $b$ and $c$ here, and the effects of
the predictors that we add in @sec-group-predictors) are called **fixed effects**. The
deviations $u_j$, which are described by a distribution, are the **random effects**, and a
model with both is a **mixed-effects model** (or mixed model). Because it describes the
data in levels, it is also called a **hierarchical** or **multilevel model**. "Random" says
that the deviations are described by a distribution; it does not mean that the plants were
allocated at random, nor that their differences have no cause.

:::: {#imp-seedlings-quadrat .callout-important title="two seedlings in one quadrat"}

The quadrats of a forest floor are either favourable or unfavourable for seedlings, each
with probability 0.5. In a favourable quadrat a seedling survives its first year with
probability 0.8, in an unfavourable one with probability 0.2, independently of the other
seedlings of the quadrat. Two seedlings are planted in a quadrat whose quality was not
recorded, and $X_1$ and $X_2$ are 1 if the first or the second seedling survives and 0
otherwise. Calculate the joint distribution of $X_1$ and $X_2$, the marginal probability
$P(X_1=1)$ and the conditional probability $P(X_1=1\mid X_2=1)$. Are the two seedlings
independent? Are they independent for a given quality of the quadrat?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

For a given quality the seedlings are independent, so their joint probability is the
product of their probabilities. The quality was not recorded, so we add these products over
the two qualities, each weighted by its probability; this is the discrete version of the
integral of the marginal density. For example,

$$
P(X_1=1,X_2=1)=0.5\times0.8\times0.8+0.5\times0.2\times0.2=0.32+0.02=0.34.
$$

In the same way, $P(X_1=1,X_2=0)=P(X_1=0,X_2=1)=0.08+0.08=0.16$ and
$P(X_1=0,X_2=0)=0.02+0.32=0.34$, which add up to one with the other two. Then
$P(X_1=1)=0.34+0.16=0.5$, and, because $P(X_2=1)=0.5$ as well,
$P(X_1=1\mid X_2=1)=0.34/0.5=0.68$. In R:

```{r}
# Probability of each quality (favourable, unfavourable) and of survival in each.
p_quality = c(0.5, 0.5)
p_survive = c(0.8, 0.2)

# Joint probability that both survive: the product for a given quality, added over the
# qualities. Then the marginal probability that the second survives.
p_both = sum(p_quality * p_survive * p_survive)
p_second = sum(p_quality * p_survive)

# Conditional probability that the first survives, for a given survival of the second.
p_both / p_second
```

The seedlings are not independent: the survival of one of them makes it more probable that
the quadrat is favourable, and so that the other one survives too (0.68 against 0.5). For a
given quality of the quadrat they are independent, by construction. This is the structure
of a grouped model: independence for a given value of the group effect, and dependence
when the group effect is integrated out.

:::
::::

# Three ways to share information {#sec-pooling}

When a parameter of a curve may differ among groups, a model can treat it in three ways.
With **complete pooling**, all the groups share one value of the parameter: the groups are
ignored and the observations are treated as independent, as in Chapter 6. With **no
pooling**, each group has its own value, an ordinary parameter estimated from the
observations of that group, and nothing connects the values of different groups. With
**partial pooling**, the values of the groups are drawn from a distribution whose variance
is estimated, as in the model of @sec-conditional: each group has its own value, the values
of all the groups inform the distribution, and the distribution in turn informs the value of
each group.

The three ways differ in what they assume and in the question that they answer. Complete
pooling assumes that the groups do not differ. When they do, the observation variance
absorbs the variation among groups, and the standard errors are too small because every
observation is treated as independent. No pooling describes the measured groups, and only
them: it says how each of these groups responds, but nothing about a group that was not
measured, because it does not describe how groups vary. Partial pooling describes the
measured groups and, through the distribution of the group values, groups in general,
which is usually the question of an ecological study (plants of this species, nests of
this bird, sites of this habitat). Its costs are an assumption about the shape of that
distribution, which is Normal in this chapter, and an integral in the likelihood
(@sec-marginal-likelihood).

For the CO₂ data, complete pooling fits one curve to all 84 measurements. The NLL is that
of a Normal model with a response curve, as in Chapter 6. The asymptote, the rate and the
standard deviation are positive, so the optimiser works with their logarithms, `log_asym`,
`log_rate` and `log_sd_obs`; the location `c0` can take any value and is not transformed:

```{r}
# Negative log-likelihood with one curve for all the plants (complete pooling).
pooled_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  a = exp(log_asym)
  b = exp(log_rate)
  sd_obs = exp(log_sd_obs)
  # Expected uptake at the concentration of each measurement.
  mu = a * (1 - exp(-b * (conc - c0)))
  -sum(dnorm(x = uptake, mean = mu, sd = sd_obs, log = TRUE))
}
```

We read starting values from @fig-co2_data: an asymptote of 30 µmol/m²/s, zero uptake
at about 50 µL/L, 63% of the asymptote reached about 100 µL/L higher (so $b=1/100$
L/µL), and a standard deviation of 2 µmol/m²/s:

```{r}
# Connect a likelihood to a data set.
cmb = function(f, d) function(p) f(p, d)

# Process the NLL, starting from the values read from the figure, and fit it.
pooled_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(pooled_nll, co2_data),
  list(log_asym = log(30), log_rate = log(0.01), c0 = 50, log_sd_obs = log(2)),
  silent = TRUE
)
pooled_fit = optim(
  par = pooled_obj$par,
  fn = pooled_obj$fn,
  gr = pooled_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
pooled_fit$convergence
```

Without pooling, each plant has its own asymptote. The parameter `log_asym` becomes a
vector with one log asymptote per plant, and `a[plant]` selects the asymptote of the plant
of each measurement, as the asymptote of each state in the practical of Chapter 6. The
rate, the location and the standard deviation are still shared:

```{r}
# Negative log-likelihood with one asymptote for each plant (no pooling).
separate_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  a = exp(log_asym)
  b = exp(log_rate)
  sd_obs = exp(log_sd_obs)
  # a[plant] is the asymptote of the plant of each measurement.
  mu = a[plant] * (1 - exp(-b * (conc - c0)))
  -sum(dnorm(x = uptake, mean = mu, sd = sd_obs, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the NLL, with the same starting asymptote for every plant, and fit it.
separate_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(separate_nll, co2_data),
  list(log_asym = rep(log(30), 12), log_rate = log(0.01), c0 = 50, log_sd_obs = log(2)),
  silent = TRUE
)
separate_fit = optim(
  par = separate_obj$par,
  fn = separate_obj$fn,
  gr = separate_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
separate_fit$convergence
```

Both fits converged. We compare the standard deviation of the measurements around the
curves, and list the asymptotes of the plants without pooling:

```{r}
# Standard deviation of the measurements around the curve(s) (µmol/m²/s).
c(
  pooled = exp(pooled_fit$par[["log_sd_obs"]]),
  separate = exp(separate_fit$par[["log_sd_obs"]])
)

# Asymptotes of the 12 plants without pooling (µmol/m²/s).
separate_asym = exp(separate_fit$par[names(separate_fit$par) == "log_asym"])
names(separate_asym) = plant_names
round(separate_asym, 1)
```

Around one common curve the measurements vary with a standard deviation of 8.2 µmol/m²/s,
and around the curves of their own plants with a standard deviation of 1.9 µmol/m²/s. So
most of the scatter around the common curve is variation among plants, which complete
pooling counts as variation of the measurements. The asymptotes range from 14.2 µmol/m²/s
(Mc2) to 45.0 µmol/m²/s (Qn3), and the three chilled plants from Mississippi have the lowest
ones. No pooling describes these 12 plants, but it cannot say how much plants of this grass
vary in their capacity for uptake, or which curve to expect for a plant that was not
measured. For that we need partial pooling.

# Maximum marginal likelihood {#sec-marginal-likelihood}

## The marginal likelihood

In a mixed model the random effects are not observed. The likelihood of the parameters
$\boldsymbol\theta$, which are the fixed effects and the variances of the model, is
therefore the probability of the observations with the random effects integrated out, that
is, their marginal distribution (@sec-conditional). For group $j$, with its observations
collected in the vector $\mathbf y_j$, this is

$$
L_j(\boldsymbol\theta)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
f(\mathbf y_j\mid u,\boldsymbol\theta)\,f(u\mid\sigma_{\mathrm{group}})\,du,
$$

where $f(\mathbf y_j\mid u,\boldsymbol\theta)$ is the joint density of the observations of
group $j$ for a given value $u$ of its random effect (the product of the densities of its
observations, which are independent for a given $u$), and $f(u\mid\sigma_{\mathrm{group}})$
is the Normal density of the random effect, with mean zero and standard deviation
$\sigma_{\mathrm{group}}$. The groups are independent, so the likelihood is the product of
the $L_j$ over the groups, and the log-likelihood is the sum of their logarithms. This is
the **marginal likelihood**, and its maximisation is called **maximum marginal
likelihood**. In plain English, the marginal likelihood of a group averages the likelihood
of its observations over all the values that its random effect could take, each weighted
by its density under the distribution of group effects. For the CO₂ data,
$\boldsymbol\theta$ holds $a$, $b$, $c$, $\sigma_{\mathrm{plant}}$ and
$\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}}$, and the integral of each plant runs over its deviation $u_j$.

Why not estimate the deviations as parameters? That is no pooling: the $u_j$ would be
ordinary parameters, and no distribution would connect them. In the marginal likelihood the
12 deviations are replaced by one parameter, $\sigma_{\mathrm{plant}}$, which describes how
plants vary. The number of parameters then stays the same however many groups are
observed, which is one of the conditions under which the large-sample properties of maximum
likelihood of [Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-likelihood-uncertainty) hold.

## The Laplace approximation

The integral of the marginal likelihood has a closed form only in special cases, such as
the Beta-Binomial distribution and the Normal linear mixed model, so in general it must be
approximated. The **Laplace approximation** uses the shape of the integrand. As a function
of $u$, the integrand is the likelihood of the observations of the group multiplied by the
density of $u$. It has a peak at the value of $u$ that is most probable for these
observations, and near the peak its logarithm is close to a parabola, so the integrand
itself is close to a Normal-shaped curve. The area under a Normal-shaped curve is known: it
depends only on the height of the peak and on the curvature of the logarithm at the peak.
So the approximation finds the peak, measures its height and its curvature, and replaces
the integral by the area under the Normal-shaped curve with the same peak and curvature.
This is the quadratic approximation of the log-likelihood that gave the standard errors of
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-curvature), applied to the integrand.

@fig-laplace shows the integrand for plant Mc2, with the parameters at the estimates of the
model that we fit in @sec-random-effects-rtmb, together with its Laplace approximation.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-laplace
#| fig-cap: "The integrand of the marginal likelihood of plant Mc2 as a function of its deviation u, under the model with a random asymptote and the parameters at their estimates: the joint density of the seven measurements of the plant for a given u, multiplied by the density of u, relative to its value at the peak (solid line). The dashed line is the Normal-shaped curve of the Laplace approximation, with the same peak and the same curvature of its logarithm at the peak."
# The model with a random asymptote, fitted as in the section on random effects in RTMB.
laplace_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  nll = -sum(dnorm(x = u, mean = 0, sd = exp(log_sd_plant), log = TRUE))
  a = exp(log_asym + u)
  mu = a[plant] * (1 - exp(-exp(log_rate) * (conc - c0)))
  nll - sum(dnorm(x = uptake, mean = mu, sd = exp(log_sd_obs), log = TRUE))
}
laplace_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(laplace_nll, co2_data),
  list(
    log_asym = log(30), log_rate = log(0.01), c0 = 50,
    log_sd_plant = log(0.1), log_sd_obs = log(2), u = rep(0, 12)
  ),
  random = "u",
  silent = TRUE
)
laplace_fit = optim(
  par = laplace_obj$par, fn = laplace_obj$fn, gr = laplace_obj$gr, method = "BFGS"
)
laplace_par = as.list(laplace_fit$par)

# Logarithm of the integrand for plant Mc2 (plant 11) at the estimates.
mc2 = co2_data$plant == 11
log_integrand = function(u) {
  sapply(u, function(v) {
    mu = exp(laplace_par$log_asym + v) *
      (1 - exp(-exp(laplace_par$log_rate) * (co2_data$conc[mc2] - laplace_par$c0)))
    sum(dnorm(x = co2_data$uptake[mc2], mean = mu, sd = exp(laplace_par$log_sd_obs),
              log = TRUE)) +
      dnorm(x = v, mean = 0, sd = exp(laplace_par$log_sd_plant), log = TRUE)
  })
}

# Peak, and curvature of the logarithm at the peak from a second difference.
u_peak = optimize(function(v) -log_integrand(v), interval = c(-3, 3))$minimum
step = 1e-4
curvature = -(log_integrand(u_peak + step) - 2 * log_integrand(u_peak) +
  log_integrand(u_peak - step)) / step^2

# Areas under the integrand and under its approximation, both relative to the peak.
area_exact = integrate(
  function(v) exp(log_integrand(v) - log_integrand(u_peak)),
  lower = u_peak - 1, upper = u_peak + 1, rel.tol = 1e-10
)$value
area_laplace = sqrt(2 * pi / curvature)
laplace_ratio = area_laplace / area_exact

# Both curves on a grid around the peak.
u_grid = seq(from = u_peak - 4 / sqrt(curvature), to = u_peak + 4 / sqrt(curvature),
             length.out = 200)
laplace_curves = data.frame(
  u = rep(u_grid, times = 2),
  value = c(
    exp(log_integrand(u_grid) - log_integrand(u_peak)),
    exp(-curvature * (u_grid - u_peak)^2 / 2)
  ),
  curve = rep(c("Integrand", "Laplace approximation"), each = length(u_grid))
)

ggplot(laplace_curves, aes(x = u, y = value, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c("Integrand" = "solid", "Laplace approximation" = "dashed")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Deviation of plant Mc2, u (log scale of the asymptote)",
    y = "Integrand relative to its peak",
    linetype = NULL
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The two curves almost coincide; the integrand has a slightly longer tail towards low values
of $u$, which the symmetric approximation cannot follow. The area under the approximation is
`r round(100 * (1 - laplace_ratio), 1)`% smaller than the area under the integrand, which
changes the log-likelihood of the plant by `r round(abs(log(laplace_ratio)), 3)`. The
approximation is accurate when the integrand is close to a Normal-shaped curve: when each
group has many observations, so that the likelihood of the group dominates the integrand,
and when the observations are Normal, or close to Normal, for a given value of the random
effect. For the Normal linear mixed models of the
[`glmmTMB` supplement](../Supplements/canned.qmd#sec-glmmtmb) it is exact, because there the
logarithm of the integrand is a parabola. It is less accurate when the groups have few
observations, and when the observations are counts near zero or binary outcomes, for which
the integrand can be skewed.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" icon=false title="Statistical detail: the Laplace approximation"}
Let $h(u)=\log\left(f(\mathbf y_j\mid u)\,f(u)\right)$ be the logarithm of the integrand of
one group, as a function of its random effect $u$, with its maximum at $\hat u$. Close to
$\hat u$, $h$ is replaced by a parabola. The first derivative of $h$ is zero at a maximum,
so

$$
h(u)\approx h(\hat u)-\frac{1}{2}\left(-h''(\hat u)\right)(u-\hat u)^2,
\qquad
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{h(u)}\,du\approx e^{h(\hat u)}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(-h''(\hat u)\right)(u-\hat u)^2}\,du
=e^{h(\hat u)}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{-h''(\hat u)}},
$$

where $-h''(\hat u)$ is the curvature of $h$ at its maximum, and the last integral is the
area under a Normal-shaped curve with variance $1/(-h''(\hat u))$, which is the constant
that is missing from a Normal density with that variance. In plain English, the integral is
replaced by the height of the peak times its width.

When the random effects form a vector $\mathbf u$ with $q$ elements, the curvature becomes
the Hessian matrix $\mathbf H$ of $-h$ at its maximum (see the box on the Hessian in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-curvature)), and $\sqrt{2\pi/(-h''(\hat u))}$
becomes $(2\pi)^{q/2}/\sqrt{\det(\mathbf H)}$, where the determinant $\det(\mathbf H)$
measures how sharply the integrand peaks in all directions together. When the groups are
independent, the matrix has non-zero elements only on its diagonal, and the approximation
is the product of the approximations of the groups.
:::

## Random effects in RTMB {#sec-random-effects-rtmb}

In RTMB we do not write the marginal likelihood ourselves. We write the **joint NLL** of the
observations and the random effects, minus the logarithm of their joint density,

$$
-\log\left(f(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf u,\boldsymbol\theta)\right)
-\log\left(f(\mathbf u\mid\sigma_{\mathrm{group}})\right),
$$

that is, minus the log density (or log probability) of the observations for given random
effects plus minus the log density of the random effects (the joint density is the
conditional density times the marginal one, @sec-conditional). `MakeADFun()` then integrates
the random effects out. Three things change compared with the NLLs of Chapters 4 and 6:

- the random effects are an element of the list of parameters, a vector with one starting
  value for each group (usually zero);
- the NLL adds minus the log density of the random effects to minus the log density (or log
  probability) of the observations, and the line with the density of the random effects
  comes before the line that uses them (we need this order to simulate from the model);
- the argument `random` of `MakeADFun()` names the elements of the list of parameters that
  are random effects, here `random = "u"`. RTMB then integrates them out with the Laplace
  approximation: the elements `fn` and `gr` of the object are the marginal NLL and its
  gradient, as functions of the other parameters only, and `par` holds only those other
  parameters.

So the fit with `optim()` works as before. For the CO₂ data the NLL is the no-pooling NLL
with the vector `log_asym` replaced by one parameter `log_asym` plus the deviations `u`, and
with the density of `u`, whose standard deviation $\sigma_{\mathrm{plant}}$ is optimised as
`log_sd_plant`:

```{r}
# Joint negative log-likelihood with a random asymptote.
mixed_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  sd_plant = exp(log_sd_plant)
  # Minus the log density of the deviations of the plants, before they are used.
  nll = -sum(dnorm(x = u, mean = 0, sd = sd_plant, log = TRUE))
  # Asymptote of each plant, and minus the log density of the measurements for given u.
  a = exp(log_asym + u)
  b = exp(log_rate)
  sd_obs = exp(log_sd_obs)
  mu = a[plant] * (1 - exp(-b * (conc - c0)))
  nll - sum(dnorm(x = uptake, mean = mu, sd = sd_obs, log = TRUE))
}
```

The deviations start at zero, and $\sigma_{\mathrm{plant}}$ at 0.1 (plants that differ by
about 10%). We process the NLL with `random = "u"` and fit it:

```{r}
# Process the joint NLL; random = "u" integrates the deviations out of the likelihood.
mixed_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(mixed_nll, co2_data),
  list(
    log_asym = log(30), log_rate = log(0.01), c0 = 50,
    log_sd_plant = log(0.1), log_sd_obs = log(2), u = rep(0, 12)
  ),
  random = "u",
  silent = TRUE
)

# Minimise the marginal NLL with BFGS: par holds only the five other parameters.
mixed_fit = optim(
  par = mixed_obj$par,
  fn = mixed_obj$fn,
  gr = mixed_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
mixed_fit$convergence
mixed_fit$par
```

The fit converged, and the estimates are those of the five parameters of
$\boldsymbol\theta$; the deviations of the plants are not among them, because they were
integrated out.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" icon=false title="Technical detail: what RTMB does with random effects"}
Each time the optimiser calls `fn` with values of $\boldsymbol\theta$, RTMB first carries
out an **inner optimisation**: it minimises the joint NLL over $\mathbf u$ for these values,
which gives the peak $\hat{\mathbf u}$ of the integrand, with Newton's method (an
optimiser that uses second derivatives; see [Chapter 8](../Chapter_8/Theory.qmd)). Automatic
differentiation ([Chapter 6](../Chapter_6/Theory.qmd#sec-makeadfun)) supplies the first
and second derivatives that Newton's method needs, and the Hessian with respect to
$\mathbf u$ at the peak gives the determinant of the Laplace approximation. `fn` returns
minus the logarithm of the approximation, and `gr` its gradient with respect to
$\boldsymbol\theta$, which requires derivatives of the inner optimum as well and is also
obtained by automatic differentiation. So every evaluation of the marginal NLL contains a
complete optimisation over the random effects, which is why a mixed model takes longer to
fit than a model without random effects. The method is described by Kristensen et al.
(2016).^[Kristensen, K., Nielsen, A., Berg, C. W., Skaug, H. and Bell, B. M. (2016),
"TMB: automatic differentiation and Laplace approximation", *Journal of Statistical
Software* 70(5): 1–21.]
:::

## Variance components and predicted plant effects

The variances $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{group}}$ and $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}$ are the **variance
components** of the model: $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{group}}$ describes the variation among groups
and $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}$ the variation of the observations around the curve of their
group. Each has the scale and the units of the quantity that it describes, and the NLL takes
their square roots, the standard deviations. `sdreport()` works on the marginal NLL as on
any other NLL, and two values of the argument `select` of `summary()` give the two kinds of
output:

- `summary(sd, select = "fixed")`: the estimates and standard errors of the parameters
  $\boldsymbol\theta$ on the optimised scales;
- `summary(sd, select = "random")`: the **predicted group effects**, one row for each
  group, with their standard errors.

The predicted effect of a group is the peak of its integrand, the most probable value of
its random effect for the observations of the group and the estimates of
$\boldsymbol\theta$ (it is also called the conditional mode). The random effects are not
parameters, so the predicted effects are not estimated by maximum likelihood: they are
predictions of unobserved quantities. Their standard errors combine the uncertainty about
the effect of a group for given parameter values with the uncertainty of the estimates of
the parameters.

For the CO₂ data:

```{r}
# Standard errors on the optimised scales.
mixed_sd = sdreport(mixed_obj)
summary(mixed_sd, select = "fixed")

# Estimates on the original scale.
c(
  a = exp(mixed_fit$par[["log_asym"]]),
  b = exp(mixed_fit$par[["log_rate"]]),
  c = mixed_fit$par[["c0"]],
  sd_plant = exp(mixed_fit$par[["log_sd_plant"]]),
  sd_obs = exp(mixed_fit$par[["log_sd_obs"]])
)
```

The measurements vary around the curve of their plant with a standard deviation
$\hat\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}}\approx2.0$ µmol/m²/s, close to the 1.9 µmol/m²/s without pooling
and far from the 8.2 µmol/m²/s of complete pooling: the mixed model, like no pooling,
separates the variation among plants from the variation of the measurements.
$\hat\sigma_{\mathrm{plant}}\approx0.34$ is a standard deviation on the log scale of the
asymptote, so it has no units. For small values, a standard deviation on the log scale is
approximately the coefficient of variation of the quantity on the original scale (its
standard deviation divided by its mean); 0.34 is not very small, and it means that the
asymptotes of plants vary around their median by roughly a third. The estimate
$\hat a\approx30.9$ µmol/m²/s is the asymptote of a plant with $u_j=0$. Because $u_j$ is
symmetric around zero and the exponential is increasing, half of the plants have a higher
asymptote and half a lower one, so $\hat a$ is the median asymptote of plants in general.
It is not their mean, which is larger, because the exponential is not a straight line (see
the box on Jensen's inequality in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-wald-constrained)).

The predicted plant effects:

```{r}
# Predicted plant effects (log scale of the asymptote) and their standard errors.
mixed_effects = summary(mixed_sd, select = "random")
rownames(mixed_effects) = plant_names
round(mixed_effects, 3)
```

The Quebec plants have positive effects, and the chilled plants from Mississippi (Mc1, Mc2
and Mc3) the most negative ones: their asymptotes are about 31%, 53% and 34% below the
median ($e^{-0.370}\approx0.69$, $e^{-0.755}\approx0.47$ and $e^{-0.422}\approx0.66$). So
much of the variation among plants follows their origin and treatment, which the model does
not know about yet.

# Group-level predictors and shrinkage {#sec-group-predictors}

A **group-level predictor** is measured on the group and not on each observation: the
origin of a plant, the treatment that it received, the habitat of a site. All the
observations of a group share its value. In a mixed model it enters as a fixed effect on
the parameter that varies among groups, where it explains part of the variation among
groups. The random effects then describe the variation that remains among groups with the
same values of the predictors, and the variance among groups becomes smaller.

The plants have two group-level predictors, origin and treatment, each with two levels. We
write their effects on the log asymptote as a baseline plus contrasts, with an interaction:

$$
\log(a_j)=\log(a)+\beta_{\mathrm{miss}}M_j+\beta_{\mathrm{chill}}C_j
+\beta_{\mathrm{int}}M_jC_j+u_j,
$$

where $M_j$ is 1 for a plant from Mississippi and 0 for a plant from Quebec, $C_j$ is 1 for
a chilled plant and 0 otherwise, and $a$ is now the typical asymptote (with $u_j=0$) of the
baseline group, the non-chilled plants from Quebec (the first levels of the factors `Type`
and `Treatment`, which R uses as reference levels). $\beta_{\mathrm{miss}}$ is the effect
of the origin in non-chilled plants, $\beta_{\mathrm{chill}}$ the effect of chilling in
plants from Quebec, and the **interaction** $\beta_{\mathrm{int}}$ is the difference between
the effect of chilling in plants from Mississippi and in plants from Quebec. On the log
scale the effects add up, so on the original scale they multiply the asymptote: chilling
multiplies the typical asymptote of a Quebec plant by $e^{\beta_{\mathrm{chill}}}$ and that
of a Mississippi plant by $e^{\beta_{\mathrm{chill}}+\beta_{\mathrm{int}}}$, and
$e^{\beta_{\mathrm{int}}}$ is the ratio of these two factors.

::: {.callout-note title="Two ways to encode groups"}
The effects of groups defined by predictors, such as the four combinations of origin and
treatment, can be written in two ways. With one parameter for each group, each group has
its own typical value (here, four typical log asymptotes). With a baseline plus effects and
interactions, one group is the baseline and the other parameters are differences from it
(here, $\log(a)$, $\beta_{\mathrm{miss}}$, $\beta_{\mathrm{chill}}$ and
$\beta_{\mathrm{int}}$). Both have the same number of parameters and describe the same
model: they have the same maximum likelihood and give the same fitted curves, and each set
of parameters can be calculated from the other. The second form makes the differences
between treatments parameters, so their estimates, standard errors and intervals come
directly from the fit, and a simpler model is obtained by leaving a term out (the
interaction, for example). The first form makes the typical value of each group a
parameter. Which one to use depends on the question.
:::

The predictors are properties of the plants, so we add them to the list of data as two
vectors with one value for each plant, in the order of `plant_names`. We take the origin
and the treatment of each plant from its first measurement:

```{r}
# Row of the first measurement of each plant.
first_row = match(seq_along(plant_names), plant)

# Indicators for each plant: 1 for Mississippi and 0 for Quebec; 1 for chilled and 0
# for non-chilled.
co2_data$mississippi = as.numeric(co2$Type[first_row] == "Mississippi")
co2_data$chilled = as.numeric(co2$Treatment[first_row] == "chilled")
```

The NLL calculates the log asymptote of each plant from the baseline, the effects of its
origin and treatment and its deviation. It also reports, with `ADREPORT()`, the logarithms
of the two factors by which chilling multiplies the asymptote, $\beta_{\mathrm{chill}}$ in
Quebec plants and $\beta_{\mathrm{chill}}+\beta_{\mathrm{int}}$ in Mississippi plants,
which answer the ecological question of the experiment:

```{r}
# Joint NLL with a random asymptote and the effects of origin and chilling.
treatment_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  sd_plant = exp(log_sd_plant)
  nll = -sum(dnorm(x = u, mean = 0, sd = sd_plant, log = TRUE))
  # Log asymptote of each plant: baseline, effects of its origin and treatment, deviation.
  log_a = log_asym + beta_miss * mississippi + beta_chill * chilled +
    beta_int * mississippi * chilled + u
  a = exp(log_a)
  b = exp(log_rate)
  sd_obs = exp(log_sd_obs)
  # Logarithms of the factors by which chilling multiplies the asymptote (Quebec,
  # Mississippi).
  log_chill_factor = c(beta_chill, beta_chill + beta_int)
  ADREPORT(log_chill_factor)
  mu = a[plant] * (1 - exp(-b * (conc - c0)))
  nll - sum(dnorm(x = uptake, mean = mu, sd = sd_obs, log = TRUE))
}
```

The effects start at zero, the other parameters at the same values as before:

```{r}
# Process the joint NLL, integrating out u, and fit it.
treatment_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(treatment_nll, co2_data),
  list(
    log_asym = log(30), beta_miss = 0, beta_chill = 0, beta_int = 0,
    log_rate = log(0.01), c0 = 50,
    log_sd_plant = log(0.1), log_sd_obs = log(2), u = rep(0, 12)
  ),
  random = "u",
  silent = TRUE
)
treatment_fit = optim(
  par = treatment_obj$par,
  fn = treatment_obj$fn,
  gr = treatment_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
treatment_fit$convergence

# Standard errors on the optimised scales.
treatment_sd = sdreport(treatment_obj)
summary(treatment_sd, select = "fixed")
```

The fit converged. The rate, the location and $\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}}$ hardly change, because
the predictors act on the asymptote only. The standard deviation among plants does change:

```{r}
# Standard deviation of the plant deviations without and with origin and chilling.
c(
  without = exp(mixed_fit$par[["log_sd_plant"]]),
  with = exp(treatment_fit$par[["log_sd_plant"]])
)
```

With origin and chilling in the model, $\hat\sigma_{\mathrm{plant}}$ falls from 0.34 to
0.079, so the variance among plants on the log scale falls by about 94%
($1-(0.079/0.335)^2\approx0.94$). Origin and chilling explain most of the variation among
plants, and the asymptotes of plants of the same origin and treatment differ by roughly 8%.

The factors by which chilling multiplies the asymptote come from the rows of
`ADREPORT()`. As for any positive quantity, we calculate their Wald intervals on the log
scale and transform the estimates and the endpoints back with `exp()`
([Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-wald-intervals)):

```{r}
# Rows of log_chill_factor: Quebec, then Mississippi.
chill_summary = summary(treatment_sd, select = "report")

# Estimates and Wald intervals on the log scale, transformed back.
critical_value = qnorm(p = 0.975)
chill_factor = exp(cbind(
  estimate = chill_summary[, "Estimate"],
  lower = chill_summary[, "Estimate"] - critical_value * chill_summary[, "Std. Error"],
  upper = chill_summary[, "Estimate"] + critical_value * chill_summary[, "Std. Error"]
))
rownames(chill_factor) = c("Quebec", "Mississippi")
chill_factor
```

Chilling lowers the typical uptake capacity of plants from Quebec by about 10%, with an
interval that runs from a decrease of 21% to an increase of 3%, and that of plants from
Mississippi by about 41%, with an interval from 32% to 48%. So the plants from the colder
origin are hardly affected by a cold night, whereas the plants from the warmer origin lose
about two fifths of their capacity. We return to the uncertainty of these effects, with
likelihood profile intervals, later in the chapter.

## Shrinkage {#sec-shrinkage}

The predicted effect of a group is a compromise between the observations of that group and
the distribution of groups. Its observations alone would give the no-pooling estimate; the
distribution of group effects pulls the prediction towards the typical value of groups with
the same predictors. This pull is called **shrinkage**. It is stronger when the group has
few observations, when its observations are noisy compared with what they need to
determine, and when the variance among groups is small, because the distribution then says
that groups are alike. A group with many precise observations stays close to its own
estimate. Shrinkage is a form of **regularisation**: the values of many groups are pulled
towards a common value, which makes each of them less sensitive to the noise in the
observations of its group. In a mixed model the shrinkage follows from the model itself,
through the distribution of the group effects; it is not a correction applied after the fit.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" icon=false title="Statistical detail: shrinkage in a Normal linear model"}
For the Normal linear mixed model with a random intercept, $Y_{ij}=\mu+u_j+\varepsilon_{ij}$
with $u_j\sim\operatorname{Normal}(0,\sigma^2_{\mathrm{group}})$ and
$\varepsilon_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Normal}(0,\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}})$, the shrinkage has a
formula. For given values of $\mu$ and of the variances, the predicted effect of group $j$
is

$$
\hat u_j=w_j\left(\bar y_j-\mu\right),
\qquad
w_j=\frac{n_j\sigma^2_{\mathrm{group}}}{n_j\sigma^2_{\mathrm{group}}+\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}},
$$

where $n_j$ is the number of observations of group $j$, $\bar y_j$ is their mean, and the
weight $w_j$ lies between 0 and 1. In plain English, the predicted mean of the group,
$\mu+\hat u_j$, is a weighted average of the mean of its own observations, with weight
$w_j$, and of the common mean $\mu$, with weight $1-w_j$. The weight of its own mean grows
with the number of observations and with the variance among groups, and falls as the
observation variance grows. For example, with $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{group}}=1$ and
$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}=4$, a group with seven observations keeps $7/11\approx0.64$ of its
distance from $\mu$ and a group with two observations $2/6\approx0.33$. For non-linear
curves and other distributions there is no such formula, but the same quantities determine
the shrinkage.
:::

@fig-shrinkage compares, for each plant, the asymptote without pooling with the asymptote
predicted by each of the two mixed models. Without the predictors the shrinkage is almost
invisible. Every plant has seven precise measurements and $\hat\sigma_{\mathrm{plant}}$ is
large, so the measurements of each plant dominate its prediction: the largest change is
that of Mc2, from 14.2 to 14.5 µmol/m²/s, towards the median asymptote of 30.9 µmol/m²/s.
With origin and chilling in the model the distribution of plant effects is narrow, because
plants of the same origin and treatment are similar, and the shrinkage is visible: the
asymptote of Mc2 moves from 14.2 to 15.6 µmol/m²/s, about a third of the way towards the
typical asymptote of 18.5 µmol/m²/s of chilled plants from Mississippi. Mc2 moves most
because it lies farthest below the typical asymptote of its group, and because its uptake is
the lowest of all the plants: the same observation error of about 2 µmol/m²/s is a larger
fraction of its uptake, so its measurements determine its asymptote on the log scale less
precisely than those of the other plants.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-shrinkage
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Asymptote of each plant without pooling (open circles) and predicted by a mixed model (filled circles), joined by a line where they differ visibly. Top: the model with a random asymptote only, whose dashed line is the median asymptote of plants in general. Bottom: the model with the effects of origin and chilling, whose dashed lines are the typical asymptote (u = 0) of each combination of origin and treatment."
# Typical asymptote (u = 0) of the group of each plant under the model with predictors.
treatment_par = treatment_fit$par
typical_treatment = exp(
  treatment_par[["log_asym"]] +
    treatment_par[["beta_miss"]] * co2_data$mississippi +
    treatment_par[["beta_chill"]] * co2_data$chilled +
    treatment_par[["beta_int"]] * co2_data$mississippi * co2_data$chilled
)
typical_mixed = rep(exp(mixed_fit$par[["log_asym"]]), times = 12)

# Asymptotes without pooling, predicted by each mixed model, and typical.
shrink_data = data.frame(
  plant = rep(1:12, times = 2),
  model = rep(
    c("Random asymptote", "Random asymptote with origin and chilling"),
    each = 12
  ),
  separate = rep(separate_asym, times = 2),
  predicted = c(
    typical_mixed * exp(summary(mixed_sd, select = "random")[, "Estimate"]),
    typical_treatment * exp(summary(treatment_sd, select = "random")[, "Estimate"])
  ),
  typical = c(typical_mixed, typical_treatment)
)

ggplot(shrink_data) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = plant - 0.4, xend = plant + 0.4, y = typical, yend = typical),
    colour = "#D55E00",
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = plant, xend = plant, y = separate, yend = predicted),
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(x = plant, y = separate), colour = "#0072B2", shape = 1, size = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(x = plant, y = predicted), colour = "#D55E00", size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, ncol = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12, labels = plant_names) +
  labs(x = "Plant", y = "Asymptote (µmol/m²/s)") +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {#imp-chick-wings .callout-important title="wing length of chicks in nests"}

The wing length of chicks of the same age is described with a Normal model with a random
effect for each nest. The variance among nests is $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{nest}}=4$ mm² and the
variance among the chicks of a nest is $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}=4$ mm². In nest A two chicks
were measured and in nest B eight, and in both nests the mean wing length is 3 mm above the
common mean. In this model the predicted deviation of a nest is its observed deviation
multiplied by the weight $w=n\sigma^2_{\mathrm{nest}}/(n\sigma^2_{\mathrm{nest}}+
\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}})$, where $n$ is the number of chicks measured in the nest. Which
nest is pulled more towards the common mean, and why? Calculate both predicted deviations,
and calculate them again for $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{nest}}=1$ mm².

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Nest A is pulled more, because two chicks say less about their nest than eight do. With
$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{nest}}=4$ mm² the weights are $8/12\approx0.67$ and $32/36\approx0.89$,
and with $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{nest}}=1$ mm² they are $2/6\approx0.33$ and $8/12\approx0.67$.
In R:

```{r}
# Number of chicks measured in nests A and B, and their observed deviation (mm).
n_chicks = c(2, 8)
observed_deviation = 3

# Predicted deviations with a variance among nests of 4 mm² and of 1 mm².
observed_deviation * n_chicks * 4 / (n_chicks * 4 + 4)
observed_deviation * n_chicks * 1 / (n_chicks * 1 + 4)
```

With $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{nest}}=4$ mm² the predicted deviations are 2.0 mm (A) and 2.7 mm
(B); with $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{nest}}=1$ mm² they are 1.0 mm and 2.0 mm. When nests vary
less, the model expects a deviation of 3 mm to come partly from the chance variation of the
few chicks measured, so both nests are pulled more strongly towards the common mean, and
the nest with fewer chicks most of all.

:::
